DISCUSSION PAPER FOR THE TEAM

Connecting the Java grid to the outer islands: how could we simulate it with IndoTERM-E?

Options, considerations and open decisions, for a static and a dynamic simulation

Draft v1 · 13 October 2026 · CEDS, Universitas Padjadjaran

What this paper is, and is not

A basis for discussion. It lays out how the policy idea could be put into IndoTERM-E, what the model and its database can and cannot do, what the literature and the planning documents say, and which decisions we need to take before running anything.

Nothing has been simulated yet. Statements about the model come from reading the TABLO file (termener.tab, version 27 Feb 2026) and the database (aggmod.har). Numbers computed from them are marked as computed. Planning-document numbers carry the pdf page of the source. Every figure is listed in Appendix C with its source and location, tagged in the text as [C3] and so on.

Prepared for Ahmad Komarulzaman (CEDS, Universitas Padjadjaran) with Claude (Anthropic) as research assistant. Draft v1, 13 October 2026. It builds on the team's note of 12 October 2026 (Interkoneksi Grid Jawa–Luar Jawa).

1. Summary and decisions asked from the team

The idea to test is: today Java-Bali has excess generation capacity while the outer islands add new coal plants; if the Java grid were connected to the outer islands, would national CO₂ emissions fall? Seven points frame the discussion.

• The policy basis is real but the window is narrow. PLN's own plan (RUPTL 2025–2034) has the Java-Bali reserve margin falling from 44.2% in 2025 to 35.7% in 2028 and 33.1% in 2034 [C1]. Above a 35% standard the surplus is 3.2 GW in 2025, 1.0 GW in 2027 and zero from 2030; above a 30% standard it stays at 1.5–2.1 GW from 2030 (our calculation) [C3].

• The planned big link runs the other way. The Sumatera–Java link (ISJ, COD 2031) is designed to move hydro and geothermal power into Java, 1.7 GW in 2031 and 2.6 GW by 2033 [C4]. Only the Java–Bali 500 kV cable (2030) and possible Bali–Lombok–Sumbawa links point the way our idea needs [C5].

• The outer-island shortage is mostly not in the plan. The five largest outer systems are planned with reserve margins of 26–52% [C7]. New coal in the plan is 3.7 GW of mine-mouth units [C8], while captive coal for smelters, which sits outside the plan, was 19.3 GW in 2025 [C10].

• IndoTERM-E does not see surplus or shortage. In the database every technology has the same cost in every region, the base-year electricity flows between regions are not physical (41 TWh from outer regions into Java-Bali against 11 TWh the other way) [C16], captive coal is almost absent, and the sourcing elasticity for electricity is 1.0 [C17]. The situation has to be built into the scenario by design.

• The literature gives a conditional answer. A link cuts CO₂ only if the generation it displaces is dirtier than Java's marginal supply plus line losses. Official 2019 grid factors range from 0.80 t/MWh (Jamali) to 1.1–1.7 (Kalimantan grids) [C19]. No study tests our exact question [C21].

• Recommendation. Use the dynamic model for the headline result, built on the plan (baseline plan against an alternative plan, as TERM-Brazil did), after a short static stage that debugs the levers and calibrates the link. Present the result as a map of conditions, not a single number.

• A possible home in GMMI. The Round 2 specification of the model intercomparison names investment in grid capacity as an example of green spending and invites a Modeler's Choice scenario [C27]. This idea could be our contribution.

Decisions we ask the team to take (details in the sections shown)

D1 Question. Emissions only, or also generation cost (BPP), subsidy and regional distribution (the four questions in the team note)? (section 2)

D2 Direction and timing. Java→outer in the near term only, or both phases (surplus first, then outer-island renewables to Java)? (sections 2, 7)

D3 Link. Which link, how many GW, load factor, losses, cost, year? The ISJ HVDC is 200 km in the RUPTL table but 1,680 km in the ESDM release. (sections 6, 8)

D4 Database changes. Clean the electricity trade matrix, keep or change regional costs, correct units and labels? (section 4)

D5 Captive coal. New industry, grow an existing one, or a satellite emissions line? (section 7)

D6 Baseline. Which RUPTL scenario (RE Base, ARED, BAU PLTU) and which Java coal retirement path? (sections 7, 8)

D7 Static stage. Do it, and for what purpose? (section 6)

D8 Outputs and framing. Indicators to report; position as a GMMI Modeler's Choice scenario? (sections 7, 9)

2. The policy question and the evidence

2.1 The idea, as the team framed it

The baseline is a Java that has more electricity supply than it needs, and outer islands whose shortage is closed by building new coal plants. The policy is to connect the Java grid to the outer islands and see what happens to emissions. The team note adds four policy questions: the change in combined emissions and the conditions for it to be negative; the effect on the cost of supply (BPP), subsidy and PLN finances; who gains or loses by region and household; and whether the idea brings Indonesia closer to the 2040 coal phase-out pledge or prolongs Java's coal fleet.

2.2 How large is the Java-Bali surplus, and for how long?

RUPTL 2025–2034 (Table 5.86) reports the reserve margin of the Java-Bali system as the net capable capacity minus the net peak load [C1,C2]. Whether this is a surplus depends on the standard. PLN planning documents use a minimum of 30% (stated for Sulbagsel in the plan itself [C7]) and the team note cites a 35% PLN standard. Figure 1 shows both.

Three readings follow. First, the surplus is largest now and shrinks as demand grows about 4% a year while Java adds little coal capacity. Second, at the 35% standard the surplus is gone by 2030; at the 30% standard about 1.5–2.1 GW remain, which is the same order as the planned 2.6 GW link. Third, capacity is not energy: dividing the plan's 2025 energy by fuel (Table 5.143) by the capacity in Table 5.86 gives about 32% for Java's 14 GW of gas plants and about 77% for its 27.5 GW of coal plants (the team note, using other capacity figures, gets 30% and 72%) [C29]. The unused room is mostly in gas. If so, power exported from Java need not come from coal, which matters for the emission sign (section 5.3). The plan also has Java's gas generation rising 2.4 times between 2025 and 2034 (pdf p483), so this room is temporary too. ESDM figures reported in the press give a surplus of about 7 GW at end-2022 and 4 GW at end-2023 [C12]; these are secondary and use another basis.

2.3 What does the plan say about the outer islands?

On paper no large outer system is short. Table 1 lists planned reserve margins by system. The shortages reported in the field come from late projects, plant outages and grid faults rather than from missing capacity in the plan. The plan itself attributes the Sulawesi shortage to late projects (PLN and IPP), seasonal loss of hydro capacity and the non-execution of the plant relocation from Java-Bali planned in RUPTL 2021–2030 [C28]. It adds that the relocation of a Java combined-cycle plant did not happen because Java needs those units to manage the entry of intermittent renewables [C28], which qualifies the idea that Java's idle gas plants are free to supply others. The generation cost is much higher outside Java (Table 2).

Our idea therefore fits only parts of the plan: the Java–Bali–Nusa Tenggara corridor, a link designed to run in both directions, or an accelerated link built while the surplus lasts.

2.5 Coal outside Java: utility plants and captive plants

The plan adds 52.8 GW in the RE Base scenario (27.4 GW renewables, 6.3 GW coal, 7.6 GW combined-cycle gas, 4.8 GW gas turbines and engines, 6.7 GW storage) and 69.5 GW in the ARED scenario (42.6 GW renewables) [C8]. The 6.3 GW of coal is the same in both: 3.7 GW mine-mouth (PLTU MT) and 2.6 GW other, of which 2.0 GW is Suralaya 9–10 in Java. (The team note quotes the 69.5 GW total with RE Base figures; the 69.5 GW belongs to ARED. We suggest correcting the note.) Examples of planned outer-island coal: Jambi-1 (600 MW, 2030, PPA signed), Jambi-2 (600 MW, 2032), Kalselteng 3 (200 MW, 2029) [C9]. Cancelling a unit with a signed PPA triggers termination costs.

Captive plants for smelters are a different order of magnitude. CREA and Global Energy Monitor count 19.3 GW operating in 2025, 4.49 GW added in the year to July 2025 (about 80% of all coal additions), concentrated in Central Sulawesi and North Maluku, and a pipeline that could take the total above 31 GW [C10]. Captive plants are not on the national grid, are outside the RUPTL, and are excluded from the JETP plan. The 3.7 GW of mine-mouth coal that a Java surplus could displace is one fifth of the captive fleet, and it sits in Sumatera and Kalimantan, away from the eastern corridor. ESDM's own roadmap says that supplying smelters by interconnection needs further study [C11].

2.6 What this means for the question

• The surplus window is short (to about 2028 at the 35% standard) and may close before a link is built; a link that runs in both directions is a no-regret investment but changes what the model must show.

• The coal that grows fastest outside Java is captive, which a grid link cannot displace unless the smelters connect.

• The emission effect is therefore a conditional result. We propose to frame the paper as: under which conditions does connecting Java to the outer islands lower CO₂, and by how much?

How this paper relates to the team note of 12 October

Confirmed against the RUPTL pages: the reserve-margin path of Java-Bali and Sumatera, the ISJ direction and size, the Java–Bali 500 kV cable year, and the scale of captive coal [C1,C4,C5,C10].

Added: the model and database findings (section 4); the surplus computed at 30% and 35% standards, where the 35% surplus is gone by 2030 rather than about 2028 (Figure 1); PLN's generation cost by system (Table 2); official grid emission factors; the plan's own statement that the Java combined-cycle relocation was not done because those units manage intermittent renewables [C28].

To correct or check: the 69.5 GW addition belongs to the ARED scenario, not RE Base (52.8 GW) [C8]; the two RUPTL tables give different Java-Bali energy mixes for 2025 (Table 5.86 against Table 5.143) [C29]; the ESDM oversupply figures and the March 2023 proposal rest on news pages we could not open.

3. The tools: IndoTERM-E and its database

3.1 How electricity works in the model

IndoTERM-E is a TERM model: a bottom-up multi-regional CGE in which every region has its own industries, households, investors and government, and goods are traded between regions on delivered prices. The energy extension of February 2026 adds fuel, energy and capital-energy nests in production and CO₂ accounting by fuel and user. Electricity has two layers (Figure 3). Seven generator industries in each region (coal, gas, diesel, hydro, geothermal, solar, wind) make a single commodity, ElecGen; they are substitutes with an elasticity of 10. ElecGen is sourced across regions by a CES choice with elasticity 1.0, and bought by the ElecDist industry, which sells ElecDist (transmission, distribution and retail) to all users.

Regional sourcing (the step our policy touches). For each commodity c, source s (domestic or imported), origin region r and destination d, the model writes the percentage change in the quantity shipped as

xc,s,r,d−ac,s,r,d=xuse+tc,s,r,d−t¯c,s,d−σc(pdel+ac,s,r,d−puse)x_{c,s,r,d} - a_{c,s,r,d} = x_{use} + t_{c,s,r,d} - {\overline{t}}_{c,s,d} - \sigma_{c}\left( p_{del} + a_{c,s,r,d} - p_{use} \right) (1)

Here x is the quantity, a the iceberg-cost shifter (atrad), t the sourcing-taste shifter (srctwist), σ the sourcing elasticity (SIGMADOMDOM), pdel the delivered price from r to d and puse the price index of the regional composite (TAB lines 1349–1362). The index is a value-share-weighted average:

puse=∑rSr(pdel+a)p_{use} = \sum_{r}^{}{S_{r}\left( p_{del} + a \right)} (2)

A negative shock to a for Java-origin electricity lowers the delivered price of Java power in destination d and, with elasticity σ, shifts sourcing towards Java. Because electricity is traded by value share and σ is 1.0, the shift is small unless the shock is large (section 6).

3.2 What the database contains

The database is the IndoTERM 2016 IO table (185 sectors) aggregated to 28 commodities, 34 industries and six regions: Sumatera, Java-Bali, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Nusa Tenggara-Maluku and Papua. As the team recalls, it was calibrated to 2022 GDP; the TABLO file still carries a 2016 exchange rate and “2016 price” labels, so the price year needs confirming. The electricity sector was split from a single sector using PLN's 2022 generation-cost shares by technology (elecost.tab). Generation by technology and region is in the header REEG, which is labelled GWh but is in MWh (it sums to 353 TWh) [C14].

4. What the model cannot see: issues to resolve before any run

Reading the TAB file and the database against the planning documents shows eight issues. Each is stated as a fact or as a hypothesis to check.

4.1 No surplus and no shortage

The model is demand-driven: output of each industry follows demand, capital is a stock that earns a rental, and there is no engineering capacity limit, reserve margin or dispatch order. Costs per technology are equal across regions, so a Java generator is no cheaper at the margin than an outer-island one. Regional average costs differ only through the technology mix, and these gaps happen to resemble PLN's: the database's average ElecGen price relative to Java is 1.20 (Sumatera), 1.00 (Kalimantan), 1.42 (Sulawesi), 3.13 (NT-Maluku) and 1.11 (Papua), against PLN's 1.21, 1.04 (Kalseltengtimra), 1.55–2.02 (Sulbagsel, Sulbagut), about 3.1 (Ambon, Halmahera) and 2.99 (Jayapura) [C13,C18]. Kalbar (2.17) and Papua are the clear mismatches. So a cost gap exists partly, but excess capacity in Java and shortage elsewhere are not represented at all.

4.2 The base-year electricity flows between regions are not physical

The inter-regional trade matrix of TERM is estimated by a gravity-type procedure and RAS scaling, not observed. For electricity it produces flows that cannot exist today: Figure 5 shows 41 TWh of ElecGen going from the outer regions into Java-Bali and 11 TWh going from Java-Bali to the outer regions; Papua sends 9.6 TWh to Java, which is 70% of its generation. The ElecDist matrix has the same problem: 15% of Sumatera's ElecDist use and 43% of Papua's are sourced from Java-Bali [C16]. The only physical inter-island link is Java–Bali (inside one region of the database).

Two consequences. A policy that “enables” a link would act on an artificial starting matrix. And because TERM changes sourcing in percentages, a flow that is zero in the base can never become positive: to simulate a new link the base needs small seed flows, or the database must be built for the connected world and the link switched off.

4.3 Electricity sourcing is very inelastic

SIGMADOMDOM for ElecGen and ElecDist is 1.0 [C17]. With constant value shares, a cost cut raises the quantity by about the same percentage, so large flows need either a large shock or a higher elasticity. Section 6 works through the arithmetic.

4.4 Captive coal is missing

CO₂ from the MetalProds industry is 0.6 Mt in Sulawesi, 0.04 Mt in NT-Maluku and 14.2 Mt in Java-Bali [C15]. The 2016 data predate the nickel smelter boom, and captive plants are in the IO table, if at all, as own-use fuel of the metal industry. The captive 19.3 GW in 2025 [C10] therefore has no counterpart in the base. (Hypothesis to check: how the IO table books captive power.)

5.2 Why models move power into Java, and what we can learn

In the decarbonisation studies the flow into Java comes from least-cost design: Java has high demand and little land for onshore renewables, while hydro, geothermal and solar are cheaper elsewhere (Langer et al.). Those scenarios retire fossil capacity to zero, so Java's coal surplus no longer exists at the end of the period; the RUPTL's ISJ has the same logic. This does not contradict the existence of a surplus today. It means the direction of value depends on the period: before large renewable build-out, surplus Java capacity can supply outward; later, outer-island renewables supply Java. From these studies we can take: the cost and loss parameters of HVDC links (US$171,000 per MW for the converter pair plus US$293 per MW-km for the cable, 1.7% annual operating cost, 96.5% efficiency per 1,000 km) [C20]; the need to treat captive and grid supply separately; and the warning that interconnection alone is not clean.

5.3 When does a link lower emissions?

Two studies of coal-heavy systems find that transmission can raise emissions. In China, expanding inter-regional transmission raised power-sector CO₂ by about 2% in 2030 because it let cheap, low-efficiency coal supply more regions (Li et al. 2016). In Europe, transmission raises emissions when renewable output is low, because it moves coal generation (Abrell and Rausch 2016) [C22]. Per MWh delivered, the effect of a link is

ΔE=EFJava(1+λ)−EFdisplaced\Delta E = {EF}_{Java}(1 + \lambda) - {EF}_{displaced} (3)

where λ is the line loss (6.2% for 1,680 km of HVDC at 96.5% per 1,000 km) and the emission factors are those of the marginal plants in Java and of the plants displaced outside Java. Figure 6 maps the sign. The team note reaches the same formula (its section 4.4).

Three lessons for the design. A link replacing outer-island coal or diesel and fed by Java coal is roughly neutral (0.80 × 1.062 against 0.87). It lowers emissions where the displaced grid is dirtier than Java's, such as the Kalimantan grids (1.12–1.67 in 2019) or Lombok (1.27). It raises emissions where it displaces gas or renewables, or if Java's marginal unit is coal while a gas unit would have been displaced. Whether the marginal Java unit is coal or gas is exactly the question the low use of Java's gas plants raises.

Further reading: evidence on when links raise or cut emissions in Appendix D2, group 1c.

5.4 CGE precedents

• Horridge, Yusuf and Ginting (2016, ADB Papers on Indonesia No. 17): the closest template. IndoTERM, medium/long-run closure (regional employment fixed through wages, rates of return fixed, trade balance to GDP fixed, exchange rate as numeraire). Connectivity is simulated as a 5% cut in road and sea transport margins plus a 1% cut in iceberg cost. The full portfolio gives benefits of about 5% of GDP (p. 3); in the first component most of the national GDP gain (0.96 of 1.09%) comes from the 1% iceberg cut (p. 9). The authors simulate only the benefits, “just half of a full cost-benefit analysis” (p. 6) [C26].

• Diniz, Ferreira-Filho and Horridge (2018, TERM-BR10, working paper marked “not to be cited”): a recursive-dynamic TERM with seven generation industries and a transmission-and-distribution industry that collects local generation and passes the surplus to other regions by inter-regional trade, the same structure as ours. National plan capacity by source, region and year is turned into investment shocks; a baseline plan is compared with alternative plans (pp. 7–10) [C26]. We use it for method and should ask the authors before citing.

• Abrell and Rausch (2016): a general-equilibrium model with explicit transmission constraints, an example of combining electricity dispatch with economy-wide effects.

• GTAP-Power and technology-bundle papers (Peters 2016; Chepeliev 2023; Cai and Arora 2015; Cui et al. 2020): transmission and distribution as a separate activity and the effect of nesting choices on results; Cui et al. warn that results depend on the substitution elasticities between power sources.

• Indonesian CGE with energy: Hasudungan and Sabaruddin (2018, feed-in tariffs), Hartono, Komarulzaman et al. (2020, energy subsidies, recursive dynamic), Yusuf et al. (2023, capital city and carbon, inter-regional). None models inter-island electricity flows.

Further reading: CGE and economy-wide models of interconnection and electricity investment in Appendix D2, group 2.

5.5 The gap

No study found measures whether moving Java-Bali surplus power to outer-island grids avoids new utility or captive coal, nor its CO₂ and economy-wide effect [C21]. The team note also finds no study of the emission effect of the ISJ. This is the contribution available to us, with the caveat of section 2.6.

5.6 Costs and wider benefits of a link

A plant and a link are not the same purchase. A plant makes energy and needs fuel; a link moves energy and needs a supplier at the other end, here Java's surplus. We therefore compare them twice: capital cost per MW of capacity, and cost per MWh delivered. The case is the eastern corridor (Java–Bali–Lombok), where RUPTL 2025–2034 plans 200 MW of new gas engines in Lombok for 2027–2030 (Lombok 3 and 4) and lists a 150 kV Bali–Lombok link of about 74 km (overhead line and sea cable) as still under study (p. V-322 and Lampiran C11).

Three readings. A short sea link costs about as much per MW as new gas engines (0.37–0.81 against 0.80 million USD per MW) and less than a new coal plant (1.36–1.60). Literature costs for long HVDC links are low, but Indonesian project estimates are not: the ISJ at 2.5 and Sumba–Java at about 4.4 million USD per MW cost more per MW than a coal plant. Long links therefore have to earn their keep through the energy they bring and the benefits below, not through lower capital cost.

On these assumptions the link delivers power to Lombok at about 74–84 USD per MWh against 124–156 for new gas engines. Four cautions. First, a single link can fail, so Lombok still needs local reserve and not all 200 MW of engines is avoided. Second, the Java side is priced at its average cost; the marginal cost, the free capacity on the Java–Bali 500 kV link (COD 2030) and the end of Java's surplus around 2028–2030 decide the real figure. Third, RUPTL flags the deep sea trench between Bali and Lombok, which raises cost and risk. Fourth, the cost sources use different price years. The result is a screening estimate, to be replaced by PLN's own feasibility numbers.

Benefits beyond money saved. Table 5.6 lists what a link brings that a cost comparison misses, with the evidence behind each item. Most are conditional on what the link displaces at the receiving end and what it calls on at the sending end.

BenefitHow it worksEvidenceFor a Java–Bali–Nusa Tenggara link

6. Designing the static simulation

6.1 What a static run is, and when it makes sense

A static (comparative-static) run solves the model once for a chosen closure and shows the new equilibrium compared with the base, with no time path. It is useful for three things: checking that the levers do what we intend; decomposing channels cleanly; and giving a target-year snapshot once demand growth has been imposed. It cannot by itself show avoided new coal, because in a long-run closure capital adjusts at once and there is no baseline growth path. We therefore propose it as a stage before the dynamic runs, not as the headline.

6.2 Closures

Table 8. Candidate closures

Closure Capital Labour Use
Short run Fixed in every industry (xcap exogenous) Real wage fixed or national supply curve Immediate effects; Java generators supply more only by using more fuel and labour
Long run (as in Horridge et al. 2016) Adjusts to keep rates of return fixed (gret exogenous, xcap endogenous) Regional employment fixed, real wage adjusts Shows capital no longer needed outside Java; the 'avoided coal' reading
Hybrid Fixed in Java generators; free elsewhere As long run Idle Java capacity plus outer-island adjustment (section 6.3)

Common to all: exchange rate as numeraire, balance of trade to GDP fixed, national household consumption following income. The dynamic closures in the package must be reversed for a static run (capital accumulation, dynamic investment rule and the demonstration shocks removed).

6.3 How the Java surplus and the outer-island shortage enter

Because the model ignores them (section 4.1), the situation is created by the scenario:

• Outer-island growth counterfactual (the shortage). Add electricity demand growth outside Java, for example nickel and metal output in Sulawesi and NT-Maluku and household growth, from RUPTL peak-load projections. In the no-link world, a long-run closure meets it with more outer-island generator capital: this is the 'new coal' reading. The link scenario has the same growth plus the connection; the effect is the difference between the two runs.

• Idle Java capacity (the surplus). Fix Java generator capital so that extra output does not carry a new capital cost, or raise capital-augmenting technical change (acap) in Java generators by the size of the surplus. With capital fixed, extra output is made by substituting labour and fuel (elasticity 1.26), so marginal cost rises a little; this is checked by sensitivity.

• Regional cost gap (optional). Table 2 gives PLN's cost by system. The database already reproduces part of the gap through the technology mix; a BPP-based adjustment would remove the mismatches (Kalbar, Papua). This changes the database and needs the team's agreement.

6.4 Options for the link itself

Table 9. Options A–C (the team decided to start with A as a mechanics test, then B and C)

Option What is shocked What it captures Main weakness
A. Price and sourcing atrad(ElecGen, dom, JavaBali, d) < 0 for destinations d; optionally raise SIGMADOMDOM Cheaper Java power delivered; more bought from Java; economy-wide price, income and trade effects Displaced generation spreads over local technologies (including gas and renewables); cannot say 'no new coal'; an iceberg cut also lowers the energy that must be generated per unit delivered
B. Capacity srctwist calibrated to a target TWh, with hybrid closure and outer-island growth Where output moves; outer-island capital no longer needed; emissions by region Depends on the counterfactual of 6.3; less 'CGE'
C. Both (proposed) A and B together, reported separately and combined Price effects and avoided build-out More assumptions to document

6.5 A worked example from the database

Java supplies 10.8% of Sumatera's ElecGen by value, equal to 7.2 TWh at Java's average price of Rp 705/kWh [C16]. In a partial-equilibrium reading of equations (1) and (2), with other prices and total demand held fixed, a cut of a percent in the delivered cost of Java power raises the delivered quantity from Java by

ΔQJQJ≈σ⋅a⋅(1−SJ)\frac{\Delta Q_{J}}{Q_{J}} \approx \sigma \cdot a \cdot \left( 1 - S_{J} \right) (4)

With SJ=0.108: a 10% cut gives +9% with σ=1 (0.8 TWh), +22% with σ=2.5 and +45% with σ=5 (3.2 TWh) (Figure 7). A link of 2.6 GW at 70% load, the planned ISJ transfer, carries about 16 TWh a year, or +223% of the base flow. With σ=1 no plausible cost cut achieves that; with σ=5 it needs a cut of about 50%. So the shock and the elasticity must be calibrated to the physical link, and the base flow must be re-based (section 4.2).

Calibration chain: link capacity (GW) × load factor × 8.76 = TWh; minus line losses; divided by the base flow = percentage change; solved for the shock given σ. Using the ISJ capacity, 2.6 GW, gives 15.9 TWh at 70% load; the 3.2–4.9 GW surplus of 2025 (Figure 1) gives 20–30 TWh at the same load.

6.6 Static scenario sequence

• S0 zero-shock run reproduces the base data (assertions, updated data equal to input).

• S1 mechanics test of option A: atrad −10% Java→Sumatera in the short- and long-run closures; check flows, emissions bookkeeping and the energy balance.

• S2 calibrated A for the ISJ-sized link, then option B with the outer-island growth counterfactual, then A+B.

• S3 extend to Kalimantan, Sulawesi and NT-Maluku/Papua; reverse direction (outer→Java) as a mirror case.

• S4 sensitivities: σ for ElecGen (1, 2.5, 5, 10); ElecDist cross-region trade removed; emission factors replaced by official ones; share of captive demand connected; carbon price on and off; closure.

7. Brainstorm: the dynamic IndoTERM-E simulation

7.1 Why the dynamic model suits the question

The question is about avoided new coal and the timing of a link against a shrinking surplus. The recursive-dynamic model has a capital accumulation mechanism (capital grows by investment less depreciation, with a one-year lag), an investment rule linking investment to expected returns, and a real-wage adjustment, so a baseline path with outer-island growth and a policy path with the link can be compared year by year to 2050. Cumulative emissions, the commissioning year and the effect of coal built before the link are all visible, which a static run cannot show.

7.2 Baseline

• Start from the existing GMMI dynamic set-up (the package files COMMON.CLS, BASE.BSH, POL2.CLS and the ALLINV files; 28 periods, 2023–2050). The earlier GMMI baseline grows alnd, labour productivity, households, trend employment and export quantity uniformly.

• Add the growth that creates the outer-island shortage: metal and nickel output in Sulawesi and NT-Maluku, households and services, from RUPTL peak-load growth by system (12.4 GW across five outer systems against 14.8 GW in Java-Bali, 2025–2034).

• Impose capacity additions by technology, region and year for the electricity industries from the RUPTL scenario chosen (RE Base, ARED or BAU PLTU), as POL2.CLS already does for renewable investment (xinvitot exogenous for selected generators) and as Diniz et al. did. Convert MW to rupiah using the model's own capital stock per MW; check it against the capital cost per kW (the database holds Rp 241 trillion of coal-power capital, to be set against installed coal capacity).

• Choose the baseline plan: RE Base is the plan PLN judges most likely; ARED is the accelerated renewable plan; the BAU PLTU case is a reference.

7.3 Captive coal

Because the 2016 base has almost none, the baseline needs a deliberate treatment. Three options:

Table 10. Treatments of captive coal (decision D5)

Option How Advantage Risk
i. New industry Add Elec_captive (coal) in Sulawesi and NT-Maluku; split from MetalProds; seed with 2025 capacity Captive coal becomes visible and can respond to scenarios Database and TAB change; data on captive output and cost needed
ii. Grow MetalProds with own power Raise coal use of the metal industry in line with captive capacity No structural change Emissions sit in the metal industry, hard to separate from the power sector
iii. Satellite line Compute captive emissions outside the CGE from smelter output and report them next to the CGE result Simple, transparent No economic feedback; a link cannot displace it unless an assumption is added

7.4 Policy shocks

• The link: a ramp of atrad and srctwist over the commissioning years (RUPTL: ISJ 2031, JBC cable 2030; a news report of 1 October 2026 quotes a 2032–2035 target for inter-island links, secondary), scaled by GW commissioned and converted from GW to TWh by load factor.

• Avoided coal: lower the exogenous investment path of outer-island coal units that the link makes unnecessary (utility units first; captive units only under the share-connected assumption); the units with signed PPAs (Jambi-1, Jambi-2) are marked as costly to cancel.

• Java generators: utilisation rises when Java supplies outward. Report the ratio of output to capital for Java generators and bound it by a check, or keep Java capital fixed in the closure.

• The cost of the link: add the investment (about US$4.28 bn for the Sumatera–Java route per ESDM; converter and cable cost per Langer et al.) as construction demand and as capital in ElecDist, financed under the chosen closure. Without it only benefits are shown.

• Direction: run a second scenario with the later phase in which the link evacuates outer-island renewables to Java.

7.5 Closures, macro and other considerations

• Investment and savings: national investment follows the baseline (invslack exogenous, as in POL2.CLS) or follows GDP (COMMON.CLS); the choice decides whether link investment crowds out other investment.

• External balance: balance-of-trade share of GDP fixed (houslack) or exchange-rate adjustment (TERM-Brazil let foreign savings finance electricity investment, causing appreciation).

• Labour: national real-wage adjustment mechanism (delfwage) with trend employment; regional migration by wage differences.

• Rebound and leakage: cheaper outer-island power may expand energy-intensive industry there; report emissions by region and by user, not only by the power sector. The team note's ‘Sumatera paradox’ (Sumatera exports to Java while adding mine-mouth coal) shows why the combined emissions of the connected regions are the right measure.

• Java coal retirement: the surplus depends on Java's coal fleet; run the link under two paths (fleet retained; early retirement under the JETP plan; press reports say the early retirement of Cirebon-1 was dropped, a secondary source).

• Carbon price: with and without delco2taxrate, since Atmo et al. find that carbon pricing changes the sign for ASEAN trade.

• Baseline calibration: compare baseline CO₂ with the official energy GHG inventory and RUPTL emissions (309 to 374 Mt for PLN plants 2025–2034 in the team note) before using it.

• Technical: RunDynam in C:\gmmi\regdyn with Base, Rerun and Policy names; results combined with cmbhar; start with a zero-shock policy file to confirm policy equals baseline.

7.6 Outputs to report

CO₂ by region and by user, annual and cumulative 2025–2050, for baseline and policy; generation by technology and region; avoided outer-island coal and diesel capital; GDP, consumption and real wages by region; electricity price by region; and the regime map of section 5.3 filled in with model results. Where the model cannot produce a number (cost of supply to PLN, subsidy), say so.

9. Data, calibration and verification plan

• Evidence ledger from the RUPTL (Kepmen ESDM 188.K/TL.03/MEM.L/2025), PLN statistics, RUKN and official emission factors: reserve margin and peak by system, capacity and generation by region and technology, planned additions, links with GW and direction, BPP by system. Every figure with page and link.

• Open items already known: capacity of ISJ per direction and whether bidirectional; heat rates by plant; actual reserve margins in 2025–2026; the two ESDM news items (oversupply and the March 2023 Java→Sumatera proposal), which we could read only through search summaries; take-or-pay terms; the basis of the RUPTL emission rows.

• Model checks: zero-shock reproduction; accounting identities; electricity balance (change in generation equals TWh moved); CO₂ bookkeeping (change in national emissions equals the sum over regions and users, with the power part split by fuel); comparison with Langer et al. (cost effects) and CREA/GEM (captive scale).

• Reporting rule: every number in a deliverable has a source, page or table, and link; results from the model are reported only after the checks pass.

Appendix A. Key relations of the model used in this paper

Equations (1) and (2) are in section 3.1 and equation (4) in section 6.5. Two further relations matter for the dynamic run. Capital accumulates with a one-year lag:

Ki,t+1=(1−δi)Ki,t+Ii,tK_{i,t + 1} = \left( 1 - \delta_{i} \right)K_{i,t} + I_{i,t} (5)

where δ is the depreciation rate (5% for every industry in the database) [C17]. Planned investment per unit of capital rises with the expected rate of return relative to the normal rate (normal gross return 13.8%, trend investment/capital ratio 9%, maximum ratio five times the trend, investment elasticity 5, partial adjustment of expected returns 0.5; the last four are identical for coal and solar in every region) (TAB excerpt 59, headers TARG, TFRO, QRAT, ALFA, RADJ). In the policy run the investment of selected electricity industries is set exogenously from the plan instead.

Appendix E. Glossary

Term Meaning
atrad Shifter for iceberg trade cost: a negative value means less of the good is lost or used up in delivery, so the delivered price falls
srctwist Shifter that moves sourcing towards one origin without changing prices (a taste shift)
ElecGen / ElecDist Commodity made by the generator industries; commodity of the transmission, distribution and retail industry
CES Constant elasticity of substitution: a rule for choosing between sources by relative price with elasticity σ
Closure The choice of which variables are fixed from outside the model and which are solved
Reserve margin Capable capacity less peak load, as a share of peak load
RUPTL PLN's ten-year electricity supply business plan; RE Base, ARED and BAU PLTU are its scenarios
ISJ, JBC Sumatera–Java interconnection; Java–Bali 500 kV connection
PLTU MT Mine-mouth coal plant
Captive coal Coal plant serving an industrial site, not connected to the national grid
BPP Biaya pokok penyediaan: PLN's average cost of supply
RunDynam GEMPACK program that runs the recursive-dynamic model year by year

Appendix F. Command-file sketch for the first runs (not tested)

A starting point for the modelers, adapted from regdata/termener.cmf, regdata/LONGRUN.CMF and the dynamic files (COMMON.CLS, POL2.CLS, ALLINV*.PSH). Variable names are those of termener.tab; closures and set elements must be checked against the compiled model before use.

! ---- Static run, option A mechanics test (S1) ----
! atrad(COM,SRC,ORG,DST) is exogenous in the standard closure (termener.cmf, line 26)
Shock atrad("ElecGen","dom","JavaBali","Sumatera") = -10; ! delivered cost of Java power to Sumatera, percent
! ---- Option B: sourcing taste shift calibrated to a target TWh ----
Shock srctwist("ElecGen","dom","JavaBali","Sumatera") = <calibrated value>;
! ---- Idle Java capacity sensitivity ----
Shock acap("Elec_coal","JavaBali") = <surplus share, percent>; ! repeat for the other Java generators
! ---- Closure for a static run ----
! keep: swap phi = Natmacro("GDPPI"); swap xhouhtot = fhou; swap houslack = shrBoTnom; swap fgovtot = fgovtot3;
! remove: swap xcap = faccum; swap finv1 = finv4; Shock delunity = 1; Shock blabnat; Shock fxstocks; ashock delco2taxrate
! long run (see LONGRUN.CMF): fix rates of return (gret exogenous, xcap endogenous) and national employment;
! rename older variables to those of termener.tab
! ---- Dynamic run: policy file (.PSH), year-by-year ----
! Outer-island coal investment follows the plan instead of the rule (cf. POL2.CLS, which has this swap commented for renewables):
! swap xinvitot("Elec_coal",DST) = finv4("Elec_coal",DST);
tshock atrad("ElecGen","dom","JavaBali","Sumatera") = <yearly path>; ! ramp over the commissioning years
tshock xinvitot("Elec_coal","Sumatera") = <yearly percent change from the plan>;
